Mumbai: The Indian rupee extended its winning streak for the fifth consecutive session on Thursday, while crude oil prices tumbled as investors bet that the Democrats' sweeping gains in the US midterm elections could push President Donald Trump towards an exit from the Iran war.
The rupee opened higher by 29 paise at 94.35 per dollar against Wednesday's close of 94.64.
Meanwhile, Brent crude futures fell $1.16 or per cent to $93.46 a barrel extending the decline for a fourth consecutive session.
Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined $1.47 or 1.66 per cent to $86.65.
Both benchmarks had tumbled about 10 per cent and settled below $100 per barrel mark in the previous session.
Moreover, crude prices have now fallen nearly 16 per cent so far this week.
The selloff follows the Democrats' victory in both chambers of Congress, dealing a major setback to Trump and his Republican Party.

A Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain the US president's military options and tighten spending on the conflict, giving him a greater incentive to pursue a negotiated exit rather than risk further escalation.
US President Donald Trump also said that Washington had no immediate plans to strike Iran, as per reports.
Apart from that, crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz -- the key waterway for most Gulf oil supplies -- have recovered to close to pre-war levels, albeit at a higher cost.
The dollar index -- which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies -- fell 0.06 per cent to 101.41 after a 0.36 per cent decline in the prior session.

stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: Polls postponed in four Andhra mandals due to heavy rains
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The elections to Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituencies (ZPTC) and Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituencies (MPTC) in four mandals of Andhra Pradesh’s Eluru district have been postponed by a day due to heavy rains triggered by Cyclone Murasu.

The polls in Velerupadu, Buttaigudem, Jeelugumilli and Polavaram mandals, which were scheduled for Thursday, November 5, will be held on Friday, November 6, Eluru District Collector K Vetri Selvi said.
According to The Hindu, the Collector also directed officials to immediately shift residents of flood-affected villages to safer locations.
Police personnel evacuated residents of Koya Madhavaram, Kummarigudem, Medipally, Allurinagar and other habitations in Velerupadu mandal as the Peddavaagu stream was in spate.

Meanwhile, State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha on November 4, reviewed arrangements for the MPTC and ZPTC elections scheduled across Andhra Pradesh on Thursday, in view of heavy rains and strong winds caused by Cyclone Murasu.

The SEC held discussions with District Collectors and Superintendents of Police to assess weather conditions, accessibility of polling stations, transport facilities and the preparedness of election personnel, particularly in cyclone-affected districts.
The Collectors reportedly informed him that rainfall had subsided in most districts and that polling could proceed without major difficulties, except in a few pockets.
Punetha directed district administrations to continuously monitor local conditions and take preventive measures to ensure that voters and polling personnel were not inconvenienced.
He said decisions on any difficulties in conducting the elections would be taken based on detailed reports from field-level officials.
He also called for coordination among departments to ensure free, fair and peaceful polling, with adequate security arrangements.
State Election Secretary A Mallikarjuna said around 2.52 lakh officials and employees had been assigned election duties, while another 52,000 personnel would be deployed for counting.
Special attention was being given to arrangements in West Godavari, Guntur and Bapatla districts, which were among the areas affected by the cyclone.

stories.title: US election results could slow AI data-centre investments, support Treasury bonds: Report
stories.summary: Proposed restrictions over electricity consumption, water usage and local infrastructure costs could reshape investment plans across three major US data-centre markets
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: The US midterm election outcome could put 141 gigawatts (GW) of planned data-centre capacity at greater risk of policy restrictions, potentially slowing artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments while supporting US Treasury bonds, according to a report by ICICI Bank.
The report said Democratic victories in the governorships of Texas, Georgia and Ohio have increased the possibility of tighter scrutiny of data-centre projects.
The three states together account for nearly 33 per cent of the country’s operating and planned data-centre capacity.
The incoming governors had campaigned on proposals to pause or restrict new projects, citing concerns over electricity and water consumption, utility costs and the impact on local communities.
The three states have a combined data-centre capacity of 156 GW, of which around 141 GW is still planned and only 15 GW is operational.
Texas alone accounts for 22 per cent of national capacity, while Georgia and Ohio account for 5 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively.
ICICI Bank cautioned that the election outcome does not guarantee the proposed restrictions will be implemented, as policy changes would require legislative and regulatory support.
However, it could lead to a “potential slowdown in further investments into data centres”, rather than a nationwide reversal of the AI investment cycle.

The report also said the outcome could be positive for US Treasury markets as tighter scrutiny of data-centre projects may slow AI capital expenditure and reduce borrowing by large technology companies.
Lower investment spending could also moderate economic growth and inflation pressures, potentially reducing the need for further interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.
Following the election results, US two-year Treasury yields fell by as much as 9 basis points to 4.54 per cent before recovering to 4.59 per cent.
The 10-year yield declined by 7 basis points to 4.89 per cent before settling at 4.91 per cent.

stories.title: ECI de-links Form 6 from SIR declaration flagged by 2 Election Commissioners

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Election Commission has removed the SIR declaration from online Form 6 across all states following concerns raised by two Election Commissioners, introducing separate submission procedures for applicants.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) has completely de-linked the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) declaration from online Form 6 across all states, including those where the revision exercise is still underway.
The declaration will now be submitted separately instead of being included in Form 6, which is used by eligible citizens to apply for inclusion in the electoral roll.
The change means applicants will no longer have to fill in the SIR declaration as part of the online Form 6 process.
The move comes amid a series of changes being introduced within the poll body's internal functioning through fresh orders aimed at improving transparency and streamlining decision-making.
The ECI has also introduced changes to the way its meetings are conducted.
Meeting agendas are now being circulated in advance, while minutes are being formally issued after meetings.
These practices were not being followed earlier, according to the details of the changes.
Another significant change concerns foreign travel by ECI officers.
Officials working with the Commission are now required to seek its approval before undertaking foreign trips.
Such prior clearance was not mandatory under the earlier arrangement.
The process for developing new information technology (IT) modules has also been revised.

stories.title: Iranians celebrate setback for Trump in US election, and other Mideast news
stories.summary: Dubai, Nov 05: Iranian officials were emboldened by a stinging election setback for US President Donald Trump, and world leaders waited to see whether Washington would end the war with Iran. Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed they fired strikes on an airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. The Israeli military said it struck two suspects in Lebanon, killing one person. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here. Iran’s leaders say election shows US voters rejected Trump’s war Iranians celebrated on Wednesday after US voters, concerned about the war and frustrated over rising prices for fuel, gave Democrats control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote — a major blow for Trump and his Republican Party. Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, wrote Wednesday on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” He warned that if the US government ignores the vote for change, “it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.” But Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, dismissed thoughts that the US will change its approach to the Islamic Republic. The broader region has been on edge for weeks over whether the US will resume full-scale military operations against Iran. Talks are ongoing aimed at preventing renewed fighting. Underscoring the mutual hostility, thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a government-organized demonstration commemorating the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy. Pro-government demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” UN peacekeeping chief says Lebanon needs UN presence and urges a Security Council decision Jean-Pierre Lacroix said Wednesday that Lebanese officials fear a “security vacuum” between Israeli forces and the Lebanese army when the UN peacekeeping mission known as UNIFIL ends December 31. Lacroix, who recently returned from the Middle East, warned of the risks of leaving the two armies “sort of face-to-face” without a third-party presence. He questioned who would monitor the U.N.-drawn Blue Line separating Israel and Lebanon, prevent unintended clashes and support communities in southern Lebanon. The border region patrolled by UNIFIL has experienced decades of violence, including a full-scale war between Israel and Hezbollah militants in 2024. Israel has long accused UNIFIL of failing to prevent Hezbollah from building up its military presence along the border. Lacroix said efforts to disarm Hezbollah had failed because “there was no political will.” The United States, Israel’s closest ally, successfully pushed the U.N. Security Council to end the mission after nearly five decades. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres proposed three options in June to maintain U.N. monitoring along the border. Lacroix said unarmed UN military observers would still be authorized to operate in southern Lebanon but questioned how they could do so without protection or support. He said a Security Council resolution adopted in 2000 remains in effect. The council is scheduled to discuss it Nov. 19. Houthis claim strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia In Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday claimed without providing evidence that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh as well as several areas in southern parts of the country. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said rebels fired a ballistic missile toward the airport, causing what he described as “major damages” to the airport. He also claimed that the group fired a drone at a radar installation and a ballistic missile at a command and control center in the Jazan province. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify these claims. The Saudi information ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The Saudi civil defense issued an alert in Riyadh overnight and other warning alerts of potential “danger” in Jazan and Najran early Wednesday. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted oil and logistic facilities as well as airports in Saudi Arabia as part of their plan to fight what they describe as the kingdom’s “blockade” on Yemen. 7 killed in airstrike in Yemen, Houthis say At least seven people, including two children, were killed in an airstrike Wednesday in Yemen’s southwestern province of Taiz, Houthi health authorities said. The Houthi-run health ministry said in a statement the strike hit a house in the district of Maqbanah and also wounded six other children. The Houthi media aired footage it said was of the struck building. The footage showed a heavily damaged concrete building, with large sections of the roof and walls collapsing. The ministry blamed Saudi Arabia, which didn’t immediately comment on the accusations. It was the latest deadly strike in Yemen since the country’s civil war was revived more than three months ago. The fighting pits the Iranian-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia and its ally, Yemen's internationally recognized government. Israeli drone strike on southern Lebanon In Lebanon, the Health Ministry said the strike on a motorcycle in the village of Qabrikha killed one person and wounded another. The Israeli military said in a statement that it had “struck two suspects who were observing IDF soldiers” without providing further details. The attack was the first in nearly a month as such drone strikes have been rare since a US-brokered ceasefire in late June ended the latest Israel-Hezbollah war.

stories.title: Arab parties extend a hand to try and topple Netanyahu, but challenges remain
stories.summary: Tayibe(Israel), Nov 5: A veteran Arab lawmaker in Israel says his bloc is willing to break with decades of precedent and join forces with Jewish-led parties in a shared bid to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule. “We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Arab Joint List, told The Associated Press. But any such partnership could be politically fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel's wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Netanyahu's opponents, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticise Israeli policies, but reject its identity as a Jewish state. After historic voter turnout delivered Arab-led parties a record share in Israel's parliament, Tibi said the Joint List is willing to support an anti-Netanyahu government without joining it. That could reassure Jewish-led factions that view them with suspicion and satisfy their own constituents. It would still give the Joint List major influence. Only one Arab party has ever served in an Israeli government, in 2021. But that party, Ra'am, is much more conciliatory than the Joint List and held fewer seats. Ra'am is willing to join another anti-Netanyahu government as a partner, but any such arrangement would still need the support of the Joint List. If the Jewish-led parties reject such a partnership, then it would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens,” Tibi said. The Joint List's positions put it at odds with most Israelis. --------------------------------------------------------------- Most of the Palestinian population in what is now Israel fled or were expelled during the 1948 war surrounding its creation. Those who remained were granted citizenship, including the right to vote, and today they and their descendants make up some 20 per cent of the population. Many Jewish Israelis have historically viewed Arab-led political parties with suspicion. That distrust has been reinforced by lawmakers who have defended or praised Israel's enemies. The Joint List, a coalition of three left-wing and nationalist parties, rejects what it refers to as the “racist Zionist consensus” in Israel. It calls for partnering with Jewish Israelis who support a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and east Jerusalem, territories occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. It rejects Israel's identity as a Jewish state, calling for equal rights for all its citizens. Many Jewish Israelis see that as support for the country's enemies at a time of war. Netanyahu has encouraged such sentiments, lodging unproven accusations of electoral fraud against the Arab-led parties and portraying them as a threat to national security. A dilemma for Netanyahu's opponents --------------------------------------------- That creates a dilemma for Netanyahu's main opponents, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot. In the campaign, they portrayed Netanyahu as a corrupt leader who failed to prevent the October 7, 2023, attack and then blocked a public inquiry into it. They cast the election in existential terms, saying Netanyahu's far-right government threatened Israel's democratic institutions. They won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared to 53 for Netanyahu's coalition. The Joint List won 11 seats and Ra'am won 8, making them crucial to forming an anti-Netanyahu majority. The Joint List could help an anti-Netanyahu bloc take power by voting for it or by abstaining to lower the threshold needed for a majority. Either arrangement could allow opposition parties to form a government without requiring the Joint List to become part of their administration. Joining could put its lawmakers in the uncomfortable position of being part of a government waging wars in Gaza and Lebanon that they oppose. Some of Eisenkot's allies welcome Arab support while others are opposed, pointing to past statements by Joint List leaders they argue deny Israel's legitimacy or support its enemies. Tibi said he was under no illusions that a partnership with Netanyahu's opponents would end the wars or bring about a Palestinian state. But he said a “repair government” would improve the lives of Palestinian citizens, by ending Netanyahu's rule and also potentially addressing local issues like a wave of violent crime in Arab communities. It's unclear what conditions would be required -------------------------------------------------- Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties must meet certain conditions in any partnership, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed. Tibi said the conditions do not apply to parties like the Joint List that want to provide outside support. The Joint List and Ra'am have denounced Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack and any violence against civilians. But they have refused to brand Hamas a terrorist group or call for its destruction, saying that doing so would justify Israel's devastating military campaign in Gaza. Tibi said both the October 7 attack and Israel's response to it were immoral. The veteran lawmaker has long been a lightning rod for right-wing attacks on Arab parties. During Israel's 2019 elections, Netanyahu, popularly known as Bibi, campaigned on the slogan “Bibi or Tibi?” to warn voters that opposing him meant relying on Arab-led parties to form a government. Tibi said Tuesday that the election result had turned the slogan on its head. “When he said Bibi or Tibi,' he incited against Arabs,” he said. “Now, it's Tibi,' because Arab voters went in a very massive way to take part in the elections. It's definitely our story this time.”

stories.headline: Questioning Democratic Institutions
stories.title: Questioning Democratic Institutions
stories.summary: The Congress party's relentless campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls exposes a familiar pattern in its political conduct: questioning democratic institutions whenever their functioning does not suit its political narrative. A party that has spent years questioning electoral transparency and accusing others of undermining democracy now finds itself uncomfortable with an exercise designed to strengthen the very foundation of free and fair elections. For Congress, electoral reforms appear welcome only when they serve its political interests. When duplicate entries, deceased voters and questionable registrations are discussed by opposition leaders, they become legitimate concerns. But when the Election Commission undertakes a nationwide exercise to identify and correct such discrepancies, the same party raises the alarm and turns an administrative process into a political controversy. The Special Intensive Revision is not an exercise designed to benefit the BJP or any other political formation. Its fundamental objective is to ensure that electoral rolls reflect genuine voters, remove erroneous entries and protect the integrity of the democratic process. A clean electoral roll is the starting point of a credible election, and no responsible political party should oppose that objective. SIR is about cleaning electoral rolls, not deleting democracy The figures emerging from the exercise underline its scale and administrative effort. Across the states where SIR was undertaken, voters were provided between 100 and 158 days, or approximately four to five months, to complete the enumeration process. Of the country's approximately 95 crore voters, nearly 82 crore, accounting for around 88 per cent, submitted their Enumeration Forms. Approximately 13 crore entries were placed under the ASDD classification — Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate — during the preparation of revised electoral rolls. The reported figures included approximately 2.89 crore deceased voters and 1.01 crore duplicate entries. The remaining cases involved voters who were absent, had shifted or could not be traced during the verification exercise. These numbers demand serious attention. Electoral rolls cannot remain static documents carrying the names of people who have died, permanently shifted or registered at multiple locations. Such discrepancies undermine the credibility of elections and create avoidable complications in the voting process. The exercise involved extensive field-level verification. Booth Level Officers (BLOs), along with political party functionaries, reportedly made three visits to voters' residences to collect enumeration forms and verify entries. This was not simply an administrative exercise conducted behind closed doors; it involved extensive ground-level participation. Importantly, exclusion from a draft roll does not mean that a genuine voter has permanently lost the right to vote. Eligible individuals can seek inclusion through Form 6, subject to the prescribed verification process. The Election Commission has also provided opportunities for claims and objections to ensure that eligible citizens are not unfairly excluded. Congress has particularly questioned Form 7, the statutory mechanism for seeking deletion of names from electoral rolls. However, the figures cited in the BJP's compilation indicate that approximately 29 lakh names were deleted through Form 7 across a voter population of 95 crore. These applications included submissions by political parties such as the BJP, Congress, Trinamool Congress, RJD and BSP, besides individual voters. If Form 7 is a statutory procedure, its use cannot automatically be portrayed as electoral manipulation. Political parties across the spectrum have the right to flag duplicate, deceased or otherwise ineligible entries. What matters is whether every application is examined according to law and whether affected voters receive an opportunity to respond. At the same time, more than two crore voters reportedly registered their names through Form 6, demonstrating that the exercise also facilitated the inclusion of eligible citizens. The scale of participation is equally significant. More than nine lakh polling booths were covered, with over 11 lakh government officials, including IAS and PCS officers and teachers, involved in supervising and conducting the exercise. More than 35 lakh authorised political party representatives participated, including over nine lakh BJP Booth Level Agents (BLA-2s). The total number of people involved was approximately 46 lakh. This raises an important question for Congress: when representatives of different political parties, including Congress itself, participated in the exercise, is the party indirectly questioning the integrity of millions of its own functionaries by suggesting that the entire process facilitated vote theft? If Congress has specific evidence of wrongdoing, it should place it before the Election Commission and pursue the remedies available under electoral law. Political allegations cannot substitute for evidence. Congress's double standards exposed by its own leaders The contradiction in Congress's position becomes even more apparent when one examines the statements made by its own leaders on electoral revision. Congress leader Ramesh Chennithala had described SIR as useful in Kerala, referring to concerns about fake voting allegedly facilitated by the CPI(M). Congress MLA Matthew Kuzhalnadan also spoke about the removal of allegedly fake entries associated with the CPI(M), suggesting that the exercise could benefit electoral integrity. Congress MP Shashi Tharoor acknowledged the problems of duplicate registrations, deceased voters and multiple entries. He supported SIR provided it was conducted transparently and with the use of digital technology to improve electoral rolls. Similarly, Congress General Secretary Sachin Pilot has maintained that people residing illegally in the country should be removed in accordance with the law. Aam Aadmi Party leader Arvind Kejriwal, who has repeatedly questioned electoral rolls, had himself claimed in 2015 that Delhi had approximately 11 lakh duplicate voters. These statements establish an important point: the need to identify duplicate and ineligible entries is not a BJP-created argument. It has been acknowledged by leaders across the political spectrum. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, leaders associated with Congress-allied political formations have also described electoral revision as important for strengthening the democratic process. Why, then, does Congress change its position when the exercise is conducted on a larger scale? The party cannot demand clean electoral rolls in states where it sees political advantage and oppose the same principle elsewhere. Electoral transparency cannot be selective. A duplicate entry does not become legitimate because it benefits a particular political party, and a deceased voter's name cannot be retained merely to avoid political controversy. This selective outrage reflects a deeper political problem within Congress: its inability to distinguish between institutional reform and political competition. From the Emergency to Kashmir's 1987 elections, Congress's democratic credentials remain under scrutiny Congress's repeated attacks on the Election Commission must also be viewed against the party's own historical record. Its leadership frequently lectures the country on democratic values, but history contains several episodes that continue to raise uncomfortable questions about its commitment to democratic institutions. The 1975 Allahabad High Court judgment against then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi remains a defining moment in India's electoral history. The court invalidated her election over electoral malpractices. Instead of accepting the political consequences, the country witnessed the imposition of Emergency on June 25, 1975. During the Emergency, democratic freedoms were curtailed, opposition leaders were jailed, press freedom was restricted and constitutional institutions came under extraordinary pressure. The episode remains one of the darkest chapters in independent India's democratic journey. Congress cannot selectively invoke democratic principles while ignoring this legacy. Jammu and Kashmir has its own painful chapter. The 1987 Assembly election, conducted under the Congress-National Conference alliance, remains associated with serious allegations of electoral malpractice and large-scale rigging. The controversy damaged public confidence in democratic institutions and left a lasting impression on generations of Kashmiris. For a region that has experienced prolonged political uncertainty and conflict, electoral credibility is not an abstract issue. People must have faith that their votes matter and that political participation can bring genuine change. The 1987 controversy remains a reminder of what happens when electoral institutions lose public trust. Congress should therefore exercise caution before assuming the role of an unquestionable guardian of democratic values. The party's history also includes confrontations over electoral institutions. In 1993, Chief Election Commissioner T N Seshan challenged the appointment of two additional Election Commissioners and the provision for majority-based decisions. The Supreme Court upheld the three-member structure in 1995. In 2009, Chief Election Commissioner N Gopalaswami recommended the removal of Election Commissioner Navin Chawla, alleging bias. The recommendation was not accepted by the then government, and Chawla subsequently became Chief Election Commissioner. These episodes demonstrate that institutional disagreements and questions of independence are not new to India's electoral history. However, they must be resolved through constitutional and legal processes, not through political campaigns designed to discredit institutions. A declining Congress cannot blame institutions for its political failures Congress's national electoral decline deserves serious introspection. Its vote share, which stood at approximately 45 per cent in the 1952 general election, fell to 21.4 per cent in 2024. This decline reflects changing voter preferences, organisational weaknesses, leadership challenges and the emergence of strong regional and national political alternatives. Instead of addressing these shortcomings, Congress appears increasingly dependent on allegations against institutions and political opponents. Since the BJP-led NDA government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have repeatedly questioned major policy decisions and institutional processes. Rafale, EVMs and now 'vote theft' have become recurring political themes. The opposition has every right to question the government and seek accountability. That is the essence of democracy. But there is a difference between constructive criticism and repeatedly creating suspicion around institutions without establishing wrongdoing. The Election Commission of India has, over the decades, overseen hundreds of Assembly elections and more than 20 general elections. It has evolved through successive reforms, from indelible ink and election observers to electronic voting machines and more comprehensive electoral-roll management. No institution should be above scrutiny, including the Election Commission. Transparency, accountability and institutional independence must remain non-negotiable. But criticism must be evidence-based, and genuine concerns must be addressed through established procedures. Strengthening electoral democracy must rise above party politics The BJP believes that electoral reforms must be continuous, transparent and free from political interference. A voter list containing the names of deceased persons, duplicate registrations and people who have permanently shifted cannot be considered a perfect electoral roll. At the same time, no eligible citizen should be deprived of voting rights because of administrative errors, migration, documentation difficulties or procedural shortcomings. Both objectives must go hand in hand. The Election Commission must ensure that every genuine voter gets an opportunity to establish eligibility, seek inclusion and challenge an incorrect deletion. opening: The Congress party's relentless campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls exposes a familiar pattern in its political conduct: questioning democratic institutions whenever their functioning does not suit its political narrative.

A party that has spent years questioning electoral transparency and accusing others of undermining democracy now finds itself uncomfortable with an exercise designed to strengthen the very foundation of free and fair elections.
body: For Congress, electoral reforms appear welcome only when they serve its political interests.
When duplicate entries, deceased voters and questionable registrations are discussed by opposition leaders, they become legitimate concerns.

But when the Election Commission undertakes a nationwide exercise to identify and correct such discrepancies, the same party raises the alarm and turns an administrative process into a political controversy.
The Special Intensive Revision is not an exercise designed to benefit the BJP or any other political formation.
Its fundamental objective is to ensure that electoral rolls reflect genuine voters, remove erroneous entries and protect the integrity of the democratic process.
A clean electoral roll is the starting point of a credible election, and no responsible political party should oppose that objective.
SIR is about cleaning electoral rolls, not deleting democracy.
The figures emerging from the exercise underline its scale and administrative effort.
Across the states where SIR was undertaken, voters were provided between 100 and 158 days, or approximately four to five months, to complete the enumeration process.
Of the country's approximately 95 crore voters, nearly 82 crore, accounting for around 88 per cent, submitted their Enumeration Forms.
Approximately 13 crore entries were placed under the ASDD classification — Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate — during the preparation of revised electoral rolls.
The reported figures included approximately 2.89 crore deceased voters and 1.01 crore duplicate entries.
The remaining cases involved voters who were absent, had shifted or could not be traced during the verification exercise.
These numbers demand serious attention.
Electoral rolls cannot remain static documents carrying the names of people who have died, permanently shifted or registered at multiple locations.
Such discrepancies undermine the credibility of elections and create avoidable complications in the voting process.
The exercise involved extensive field-level verification.
Booth Level.
Officers (BLOs), along with political party functionaries, reportedly made three visits to voters' residences to collect enumeration forms and verify entries.
This was not simply an administrative exercise conducted behind closed doors; it involved extensive ground-level participation.
Importantly, exclusion from a draft roll does not mean that a genuine voter has permanently lost the right to vote.
Eligible individuals can seek inclusion through Form 6, subject to the prescribed verification process.
The Election Commission has also provided opportunities for claims and objections to ensure that eligible citizens are not unfairly excluded.
Congress has particularly questioned Form 7, the statutory mechanism for seeking deletion of names from electoral rolls.
However, the figures cited in the BJP's compilation indicate that approximately 29 lakh names were deleted through Form 7 across a voter population of 95 crore.
These applications included submissions by political parties such as the BJP, Congress, Trinamool Congress, RJD and BSP, besides individual voters.
If Form 7 is a statutory procedure, its use cannot automatically be portrayed as electoral manipulation.
Political parties across the spectrum have the right to flag duplicate, deceased or otherwise ineligible entries.
What matters is whether every application is examined according to law and whether affected voters receive an opportunity to respond.
At the same time, more than two crore voters reportedly registered their names through Form 6, demonstrating that the exercise also facilitated the inclusion of eligible citizens.
The scale of participation is equally significant.
More than nine lakh polling booths were covered, with over 11 lakh government officials, including IAS and PCS officers and teachers, involved in supervising and conducting the exercise.
More than 35 lakh authorised political party representatives participated, including over nine lakh BJP Booth Level Agents (BLA-2s).
The total number of people involved was approximately 46 lakh.

This raises an important question for Congress: when representatives of different political parties, including Congress itself, participated in the exercise, is the party indirectly questioning the integrity of millions of its own functionaries by suggesting that the entire process facilitated vote theft?
If Congress has specific evidence of wrongdoing, it should place it before the Election Commission and pursue the remedies available under electoral law.
Political allegations cannot substitute for evidence.
Congress's double standards exposed by its own leaders.
The contradiction in Congress's position becomes even more apparent when one examines the statements made by its own leaders on electoral revision.
Congress leader Ramesh Chennithala had described SIR as useful in Kerala, referring to concerns about fake voting allegedly facilitated by the CPI(M).
Congress MLA Matthew Kuzhalnadan also spoke about the removal of allegedly fake entries associated with the CPI(M), suggesting that the exercise could benefit electoral integrity.
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor acknowledged the problems of duplicate registrations, deceased voters and multiple entries.
He supported SIR provided it was conducted transparently and with the use of digital technology to improve electoral rolls.
Similarly, Congress General Secretary Sachin Pilot has maintained that people residing illegally in the country should be removed in accordance with the law.
Aam Aadmi Party leader Arvind Kejriwal, who has repeatedly questioned electoral rolls, had himself claimed in 2015 that Delhi had approximately 11 lakh duplicate voters.
These statements establish an important point: the need to identify duplicate and ineligible entries is not a BJP-created argument.
It has been acknowledged by leaders across the political spectrum.
In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, leaders associated with Congress-allied political formations have also described electoral revision as important for strengthening the democratic process.
Why, then, does Congress change its position when the exercise is conducted on a larger scale?
The party cannot demand clean electoral rolls in states where it sees political advantage and oppose the same principle elsewhere.
Electoral transparency cannot be selective.
A duplicate entry does not become legitimate because it benefits a particular political party, and a deceased voter's name cannot be retained merely to avoid political controversy.

stories.headline: Cabinet Approves Rs.2,814 Crore Critical Mineral Processing Scheme Till 2031
stories.title: Cabinet Approves Rs.2,814 Crore Critical Mineral Processing Scheme Till 2031
stories.summary: The Union Cabinet has approved a Rs.2,814 crore capital expenditure support scheme to establish four domestic critical mineral processing plants, targeting lithium and nickel processing, over FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31. Under the scheme, the government will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for setting up two lithium processing plants and two nickel processing plants. Each lithium plant must have a minimum processing capacity of 30,000 tonnes (30 kt), while each nickel plant must have a minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes (50 kt). The maximum capital support has been capped at Rs.500 crore per lithium plant beneficiary and Rs.900 crore per nickel plant beneficiary. The scheme aims to expand India's domestic capacity to process lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds. It also provides for the recovery of cobalt as a by-product of nickel processing. Selection and Disbursement of Incentives Beneficiaries will be selected through a two-stage process. Applicants will first undergo technical evaluation, with only qualified applicants eligible to participate in financial bidding. Two beneficiaries will be selected for each mineral based on the least-cost criterion, which means preference will be given to bidders seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government. The capital subsidy will be disbursed in three tranches, linked to the achievement of specified project milestones. Reducing Dependence on Critical Mineral Imports India currently depends substantially on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity critical mineral materials, including lithium, nickel and cobalt. Domestic processing capacity remains limited due to high capital requirements, technology constraints and restricted access to raw materials. The new scheme is intended to address these gaps by supporting domestic processing infrastructure and increasing value addition within the country. The proposed capacity is expected to support downstream sectors, including electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel, where lithium, nickel and cobalt are important raw materials. The scheme will run for five years, from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, with a total financial outlay of Rs.2,814 crore. Key Challenges that could Test India's Critical Mineral Processing Push Raw material availability: While the scheme aims to strengthen domestic processing, securing a consistent supply of lithium and nickel ores will remain a major challenge. Continued reliance on imported feedstock could limit the extent of import substitution. High capital and operating costs: Despite the 30% capital subsidy, high initial investment, energy costs and specialised equipment requirements could affect project viability. Global price volatility: Fluctuations in international lithium and nickel prices could affect raw material procurement costs and the profitability of domestic processing facilities. Demand and offtake challenges: The commercial viability of the proposed plants will also depend on consistent demand from battery manufacturers, electric mobility companies and other downstream industries.

stories.title: TN CM Joseph Vijay Writes To PM Narendra Modi Seeking Supreme Court's Regional Bench In Chennai

article_sentences: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Joseph Vijay has written to the Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, reiterating the need for setting up a regional bench of the Supreme Court of India in Chennai.
In his letter, Vijay states that when the Constitution was enacted, the framers of the Constitution wanted every citizen of the country to have access to justice.

He added that presently, the remedy under Article 32 of the Constitution was available only to citizens who were geographically closer to the Supreme Court or those who were financially privileged to meet the cost of travel and litigation.

"In this connection, I would like to add that when the constitution was enacted, the framers of the constitution contemplated that all citizens of this country, rich or poor must have direct access to the Court.
It was the main reason for enactment of Article 32, a privilege not available in many other countries.

However, over the time, the remedy under Article 32 is practically available only to citizens who are geographically close to the Supreme Court of India and who are financially privileged to meet the cost of litigation and travel.
However, citizens located mainly in the South India is deprived of availing this remedy due to the sheer distance between the Southern States and New Delhi," the letter states.

Vijay pointed out that as per Article 130 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi, or in such place of places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, decide.

He pointed out that setting up of a bench of Supreme Court in Chennai, an important place in South India would benefit all the southern states, as a litigant from south will not have to travel all the way to New Delhi to get their grievance redressed.

He added that establishment of a bench at Chennai would reflect true federal character of the Nation and will not affect the independence of the judiciary since the control over the bench would remain with the Chief Justice of India.

He also stated that the Madras High Court, one of the oldest chartered High Courts in India, had a highly professional, talented, and competent bar which would meet the proposed need of the Supreme Court bench at Chennai.

He further added that despite the State's assurance that it would provide the necessary infrastructure facilities, including residential accommodation for the Supreme Court Judges befitting their status, etc., the full court of the Supreme Court, in its meeting on August 7, 2007, had refused to reconsider its earlier decision against setting up a bench.

article_sentences: Washington: The United States has imposed sanctions on an India-based couple and several associated companies over their alleged involvement in facilitating Iran's shadow fleet through fraudulent maritime registrations and certifications, accusing them of helping sanctioned vessels transport Iranian petroleum and evade international restrictions.

Announcing the action on Wednesday (local time), US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Washington would take action against individuals and entities continuing to support the Iranian regime.
"As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us.
We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air," Bessent said in a post on X.
In a press release, the US Department of the Treasury identified the targeted individuals as India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.

It alleged that the couple operated a network providing false flags and maritime certifications to sanctioned vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including ships operating on behalf of Iran's military and its proxies.

According to the department, Sharma and Shahid allegedly established fraudulent maritime registries and classification societies by creating websites that purported to offer services on behalf of countries that had not authorised them.
The Treasury said their activities dated back to at least 2014, when they allegedly attempted to impersonate the maritime flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica.
It further alleged that their network provided registration services to vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, enabling them to circumvent international restrictions.
Several India-based companies associated with the couple have also been designated, including Oceaniek Technologies India and Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited.

Other entities named include Precept Trends Private Limited, Polynesia Maritime Private Limited, Alexarya Finserv Private Limited, Alexarya Media and Entertainment Private Limited, Viharaboating Private Limited and Aryavart Maritime and Educational Trust.
The Treasury said the sanctions were imposed under Executive Order 13902, which targets key sectors of the Iranian economy, including petroleum, petrochemicals and aviation.
